For parking information, please visit this link: https://www.dc.umich.edu/about-the-dc/maps-floor-plans-hours/#parking

Exhibition Opening Event: 
- When: Friday, September 18, 5 pm to 6 pm
- Where: Duderstadt Center Gallery
- Open to the public
- Description: Please join us for the opening of this photo exhibition. The event will feature remarks by the organizers, the exhibition curators, one of the featured photojournalists, and a former Peace Corps volunteer who has stood in solidarity with the people of Gwangju since 1980. Light refreshments are provided. 

*Exhibition Description*
This photo exhibition features 90 curated images from the UNESCO-inscribed May 18 Archives. Documenting the May 18–27, 1980 democratization uprising in Gwangju, South Korea, the collection captures the shift from peaceful student protests to military violence and unified citizen resistance, carried out under a complete blackout as civilians and photojournalists risked their lives to photograph atrocities and smuggle film past cordons. Beyond serving as historical artifacts, these preserved visual truths offer a living blueprint for popular resilience against authoritarianism, transforming local trauma into a universal defense of human rights. Displaying these records at Michigan bridges 1980 Gwangju with our present moment, inviting viewers to engage past resistance in the ongoing effort to defend democracy today.

*Exhibition Composition*
The exhibit will be composed of a visual narrative comprised of six chronological sections and two additional special sections:

1. Protest (May 5–16, 1980): 
Following the collapse of Park Chung-hee’s military dictatorship in October, 1979, Gwangju students and citizens held peaceful rallies for campus autonomy and the end of martial law. Photos from this era show orderly marches and hopeful faces, capturing a society on the brink of change before the structural contradictions shifted toward state-led violence. 

2. Suppression (May 18–19, 1980): 
A new junta government led by Chun Doo-hwan extended martial law to the entire country on May 17. Students at Chonnam National University protested against the new junta government’s decision. State violence escalated as paratroopers, who were deployed to Gwangju, engaged student protesters. Streets became scenes of brutal beatings and kidnappings. Beyond documenting victims, the images on display in this section serve as primary historical evidence and legal proof of the military's methods and the sudden transformation of citizens into targets of control. 

3. Uprising (May 20–21, 1980): 
The movement shifted into a popular struggle. Vehicles lined up in Gwangju’s main thoroughfare, Geumnam-ro. This massive vehicle parade symbolized the people becoming active subjects of resistance. The military was given the order to use live ammunition against civilians. In reaction, the city became a space of voluntary mobilization and citizens emerged as historical political actors. 

4. Resistance (May 22–26, 1980): 
While isolated and cut off from communications, Gwangju established an autonomous system of self-governance. Photos in this section testify to the efforts made to establish a sense of order based on solidarity—sharing food and donating blood—rather than chaos. The formation of this "Daedong (Great Unity) Community" and the visual documentation thereof serve as foundations of democracy in South Korea. 

5. Massacre (May 27, 1980): 
The uprising was crushed by a dawn military operation. While the armed resistance ended, the resulting photographs of the aftermath reveal the stark reality of the massacre. These images became the catalyst for future truth-seeking movements and the pursuit of historical justice in South Korea. 

6. Mourning: 
Scenes of coffins, portraits, and silent vigils represent a collective ethical gaze. During this period, mourning was more than a display of grief; it was a communal act used to redefine the city’s identity and establish new moral standards for justice.

7. Special Section A: The Photographers
This special section highlights the domestic and international photographers who documented the uprising. This includes Korean journalists alongside US journalists Robin Moyer and Norman Thorpe, French correspondents Patrick Chauvel and François Lochon, and German cinematographer Jürgen Hinzpeter. Their images transcend simple reporting, reflecting a moral commitment to record and a historical duty to ensure remembrance. Rather than viewing these photos solely as evidence, the exhibition reinterprets them through a lens of photographic history—examining their context, distribution, and how they transformed raw records into social truth and collective memory.

8. Special Section B: The Peace Corps: Americans Who Helped Gwangju
When Gwangju was isolated under martial law in May 1980, four American Peace Corps volunteers—Tim Warnberg, David Lee Dolinger, Judi Chamberlin, and Paul Courtright—refused to leave, choosing instead to assist the wounded, aid foreign journalists, and ultimately expose the truth to the world. Those pivotal ten days reshaped their lives into lifelong commitments to human rights, inspiring decades of memoirs, academic writings, and testimonies. Through photographs, video footage, and personal records, this section traces their journey from eyewitnesses to active defenders of human dignity, inviting us to reflect on what it truly means to take a stand in the face of another’s suffering.

combined_title: Multimargin Selection in Leniency Designs: Lonjezo Sithole, University of Michigan
description: Leniency designs use quasi-random assignment to decision makers with different treatment propensities to estimate causal effects. When decision makers weight unobserved case characteristics differently, a higher (lower) overall treatment rate can mask a lower (higher) probability of treating some case types. I develop a model with finitely many latent regimes, each representing a case type with its own potential outcome distributions and treatment probabilities that vary across decision-makers. The main identifying restriction is that, within a regime and conditional on observed characteristics, unobserved factors governing treatment decisions are independent of potential outcomes. Under the model, observed outcome distributions admit a finite mixture representation, and pairwise Wald estimands decompose into regime-specific treatment effects weighted by each regime’s share of the aggregate first stage. I give conditions for identifying the number of regimes, their treatment effects, and their weights using parametric restrictions on outcome distributions or auxiliary pretreatment measurements. I characterize when the weights are nonnegative and when they are constant across decision-maker pairs. I develop bootstrap tests of both restrictions and establish their pointwise asymptotic validity for a fixed number of regimes. Applying the model to Miami-Dade pretrial bail data, I find that some of the more lenient groups of judges release fewer defendants of the case type for whom release most reduces prison time.

event_subtitle: *Designing Neuroprotective Therapies for the Developing Brain*
description:
A reception with light refreshments will be held in the B10 lobby before each seminar from 1-1:30 p.m.

*Abstract:*
Therapeutics for neonatal and pediatric populations often lag years behind adult treatments, leaving clinicians to rely on off-label use of adult drugs. This gap underscores the urgent need for technologies tailored to the unique physiology of newborns and children, particularly for conditions involving the brain. Our research addresses this challenge by engineering microphysiological models that replicate the complexity of the brain microenvironment and enable systematic evaluation of therapeutic strategies. In this talk, I will highlight how we use physiologically relevant models to inform the design of neuroprotective strategies for neonatal and pediatric brain diseases. I will show a few case studies of leveraging these models to screen therapeutics, including the use of nanotechnology platforms for small molecule delivery, to advance their use in the clinic. By bridging engineering, neuroscience, and data science, our goal is to close the technology gap for children’s therapeutics and improve neurological health across the lifespan.

*Bio:*
Dr. Elizabeth Nance is the Steven & Connie Rogel Endowed Professor & Department Chair of Chemical Engineering at UW, Professor of Bioengineering, and Adjunct Professor in Radiology. Elizabeth received her B.S. in Chemical Engineering from NC State University, and her Ph.D. from Johns Hopkins University in Chemical & Biomolecular Engineering with Dr. Justin Hanes, with a focus on nanotherapies for brain cancer. She completed a postdoc with Dr. Sujatha Kannan in Anesthesiology & Critical Care Medicine at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, with training in neuroscience and animal model development. Elizabeth has received the Presidential Early Career Achievement in Science & Engineering (PECASE) award, the UW Undergraduate Research Mentor Award, an NIGMS R35 MIRA award, and the Burroughs Wellcome Career Award. She was a finalist for the 2025 Blavatnik National Award for Life Sciences and was named to the College of Fellows for the Controlled Release Society. Elizabeth serves as the Editor in Chief for Bioengineering & Translational Medicine and is a mentor with Invent@Seattle Children’s to support commercialization of therapeutics for kids.

Abstract:
Wearable brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are a promising option to provide access to technology for those with severe disabilities without requiring physical movement. However, BCIs are not yet available as a commercial assistive technology. Dr. Huggins' University of Michigan Direct Brain Interface Laboratory focuses on making BCIs practical for people who need them.  This involves identifying and solving usability issues that others have overlooked. Our BCI includes expanding capabilities to access commercial software and provides usability features designed for real-world, user-paced communication. Our in-home clinical trials and laboratory testing of BCI with real-world tasks have identified additional challenges that must be overcome to expand BCI availability and usability so that BCI can become a standard of care for those with the most profound physical disabilities.

Dr. Huggins is trained in Computer Engineering and Biomedical Engineering with degrees from Carnegie Mellon and the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. description:
AI may change how science answers its hardest open questions, and even which questions it asks. Today's vast datasets hold physical information we do not yet know how to look for, and AI offers a way to search for the unexpected. To trust AI discoveries, we need to judge models by whether they obey the laws of physics. How convincing their outputs look is not enough. In this talk I will discuss the promise and challenges of cutting-
edge AI for science, and how to define and build physical realism into our models. I will present recent progress
on physical, probabilistic, and generative models for astronomy. I will also show where classical physics
models, machine learning, and agentic AI each reach their limits.

combined_title: IES Energy Seminar Series - Prioritization of technology development and scale-up pathways for sustainable (bio)energy systems: Jeremy Guest, UIUC
description:
Abstract:
The pursuit of clean, equitable, renewable fuels has become a catalyst for research and development. Yet a critical challenge in transitioning fuel supply chains is the vast landscape of possible technology development pathways and the lack of transparent, consistent frameworks to target research and investment. This presentation will introduce quantitative sustainable design (QSD), a framework for prioritizing research, development, and deployment pathways for emerging technologies. QSD integrates process design and simulation, techno-economic analysis, and life cycle assessment under uncertainty to identify the factors governing sustainability, quantify performance gaps, establish actionable research targets, and guide technology and system design. Examples from the Center for Advanced Bioenergy and Bioproducts Innovation will illustrate how QSD can inform the conversion of perennial grasses (including Miscanthus, switchgrass, and sugarcane) and agricultural residues into biofuels and bioproducts, with particular attention to sustainable aviation fuel. By connecting process-scale analyses with broader infrastructure and spatial models, we also evaluate where and how these technologies could be deployed, including opportunities to integrate low-carbon fuel production with existing infrastructure and strategically site bioenergy facilities. Together, these examples demonstrate how transparent, systems-level analysis can direct innovation and investment toward energy solutions that are technically feasible, financially viable, environmentally beneficial, and responsive to broader societal goals.

Biography:
Dr. Jeremy Guest is the Department Head and David C. Crawford Faculty Scholar in the Department of Civil & Environmental Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He also holds an appointment (by courtesy) as a Professor in the Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering. The core goal of Professor Guest’s research group is to advance circular bioeconomies for a more sustainable and just future. His team supports this vision by developing computational models to prioritize research, development, and deployment pathways for new technologies that achieve resource recovery from wastewaters and the conversion of plants to products, food, and fuels. Professor Guest’s formal training includes a B.S. and M.S. in civil engineering from Bucknell University and Virginia Tech, respectively, and a Ph.D. in environmental engineering from the University of Michigan.

Despite this growth, some datasets remain inherently limited; including many derived from specimens from natural history collections. In this talk, Bryan Carstens will discuss the potential of Artificial Intelligence approaches to improve biological datasets. One example describes the application of transfer learning to improve the genomic data collected from specimens where the sampling is inherently limited, such as from extinct species. A second describes the use of neutral networks to automate pseudo-landmarks in three dimensional geometric morphometrics. Taken together, this work suggests that AI has the potential to enhance biological data, leading to increased inferential capabilities.

combined_title: EIHS Lecture: Imagine Lagos: Rethinking the Histories of West African Cities in the Nineteenth Century: Ademide Adelusi-Adeluyi (Howard University)
description:
Urban questions have taken on a new urgency, as cities like Lagos grow faster and more intensely, seemingly every day. But how should we understand the ways the past shaped and produced this present? And how can, or should we, write and map the histories of people rooted in oral cultures? This presentation explores the premise that reading Lagos’s streets shapes the ways to ask, analyze and frame nineteenth-century narratives of the city. By drawing new maps of Lagos and the lagoon, I transcribe the answers to these questions as they were understood and framed in the city’s social geography.

Trained as both historian and computer engineer, Ademide’s research into the history of West African cities combines a set of interdisciplinary interests in maps, mapmaking, and digital humanities. Her first book, Imagine Lagos, explores the city’s 19th-century history. It was awarded the Best Book Prize in 2024 by the African Studies Association and is a finalist for the Association for the Study of the Worldwide African Diaspora’s Outstanding First Book award. She a founding member of the Lagos Studies Association, and is Associate Professor of History at Howard University (where she is also a faculty affiliate of the Black Data Lab).

This event presented by the Eisenberg Institute for Historical Studies. It is made possible in part by a generous contribution from Kenneth and Frances Aftel Eisenberg.

“How many workshops do I have to sign up for?”
You only need to sign up for 1 workshop. Attending 1 workshop will fulfill the requirement for the training. 
“I see that there is more than one session, does it matter which one I sign up for?”
It generally does not matter which workshop you sign up for. There will be a few that are designated for specific groups such as transfer students or for students looking for accommodations. This workshop is required for all transfer and first-year students at the University of Michigan.
“I’ve experienced harm around relationships or sexual experiences in the past and I am worried that attending this workshop may be harmful for me.” 
Our team is aware that students who are coming into the university that have experienced harm in the past. Our workshop is specifically designed to respect and validate the experiences of survivors and has been carefully constructed to avoid any specific descriptions of violence and focus instead on themes of empowerment, communication, and boundary setting. However, if you still have concerns about programming and would like to request alternative programming, please feel free to reach out at organizer17@example.edu.
“What if I struggle to learn in a presentation setting? I’m an active learner.”
Our workshop is built to meet a variety of learning styles, including time for self-reflection, small group sharing, and resources to take with you to work through on your own time! This workshop is meant to be interactive and inclusive. 
“Can I request accommodations?”
We considered accessibility in creating this workshop and selecting the locations in which the workshops are help. In this case, please sign up for another workshop as soon as you can as the workshop is required and may fill up especially near the end of the semester. No need to contact SAPAC unless you are not able to reschedule. 
“I have had gender-based violence training before, can I get this requirement waived?”
As this workshop was designed with University of Michigan student feedback in mind, our workshop is unique to the UM community. Our curriculum focuses on individualized reflection and because of its interactive nature, each workshop will be unique to the people attending. Although we are excited you already have familiarity with the subject, this workshop is required for every first year and transfer student. 
“I’m a commuter/non-traditional student, do I still have to attend?"
Yes, this workshop is required for every first-year and transfer student - not only do we want every student to benefit from having this time to connect with peers, but we also want to make sure your peers benefit from what you bring to our community. combined_title: Imagining Palestine-Israel: A Conversation with Maurice Ebileeni (University of Haifa) and Shachar Pinsker (University of Michigan), Moderated by Maya Barzilai (University of Michigan)
event_subtitle: A Conversation with Maurice Ebileeni (University of Haifa) and Shachar Pinsker (University of Michigan), Moderated by Maya Barzilai (University of Michigan)
description:
We invite you to a moderated conversation around a forthcoming special issue of the journal Palestine/Israel Review, titled “Imagining Palestine-Israel” guest-edited by Ebileeni and Pinsker.

The call for papers from spring 2024 stated that in thinking about Palestine-Israel, to imagine is both problematic and crucial insofar as imagination might offer different and new horizons and futures or further preserve the political impasse as well as diverge from the atrocities of the present into even more dangerous territories. The editors also raised some of the following questions:

– Is it possible to envision a way forward in this present moment?
– Is it possible to imagine together an equitable future that will account for the atrocities and injustices of the past and still make room for a Palestine and an Israel on the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea?
– Is a dialogue based on honesty and accountability possible at all anymore?
– Are dialogues about Palestine and Israel in academia at all beneficial?

Scholars across various disciplines (literary and cultural studies, anthropology, history), from around the globe, responded to the call and these questions. They tried to make sense of the ever-escalating destruction of Gaza, and to engage in the difficult task of imagining what the future could look like.

Now, two years after the “Imagining Palestine-Israel” scholarly initiative started, amidst a US and Israeli-led war on Iran and its subsidiary front with Lebanon, the questions we raised back in 2024 are even more relevant.

combined_title: Nilima Sheikh: Picturing the Other: In conversation with Rattanamol Singh Johal
event_subtitle: In conversation with Rattanamol Singh Johal
description:
Join acclaimed visual artist Nilima Sheikh for a conversation with Rattanamol Singh Johal about her artistic practice and engagement with traditional Indian art forms and literary sources. The conversation will be followed by an audience Q&A.

Nilima Sheikh’s work focuses on displacement, loss, longing, violence, the perception of tradition and ideas of femininity. Her artworks, using tempera on handmade paper or canvas, are influenced by Persian, Central Asian, Far Eastern, pre-Renaissance European and North Indian schools of painting. Her visual and textual layering, informed by a mix of lore and history, offers glimpses into multiple worlds, and a commitment to feminist realities.

Nilima Sheikh was born in New Delhi, India in 1945. After graduating in History from Delhi University, she studied Painting at the Faculty of Fine Arts, MS University of Baroda between 1965 and 1971 under the mentorship of Professor KG Subramanyan. Her work explores historical art forms through the lens of personal subjectivities, using a range of visual and literary sources. Working at different scales and on varied surfaces, her contemporary practice critically engages a wide range of visual methods, materials and styles.

Sheikh's solo exhibition 'Fractured Skies' at The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York will be on view from September 27, 2026 through June 13, 2027. Recent exhibitions include 'The Imaginary Institution of India' at the Barbican Centre in London (2024), the Sharjah Biennial 15 titled 'Thinking Historically in the Present' (2023), the Dhaka Art Summit (2020), the Kochi-Muziris Biennale (2018), Documenta 14 in Kassel and Athens (2017), and 'Each night put Kashmir in your dreams' at the Art Institute of Chicago (2014). Sheikh's writings have been published widely, she has created scenography for theatre, and also illustrated books for children. 

This event is made possible by the Shireen and Afzal Ahmad South Asian Arts Programming Fund.

combined_title: The DAAS Zora Neale Hurston Lecture of the Humanities with Edda Fields-Black (Carnegie Mellon): COMBEE: Harriet Tubman, the Combahee River Raid, and Black freedom During the Civil War
event_subtitle: COMBEE: Harriet Tubman, the Combahee River Raid, and Black freedom During the Civil War
description:
Edda L. Fields-Black is an American historian who is Professor of History and Director of the Dietrich College Humanities Center at Carnegie Mellon University. She won the 2025 Pulitzer Prize in History for her book COMBEE: Harriet Tubman, the Combahee River Raid, and Black Freedom during the Civil War. 

Summary
Harriet Tubman's legendary life is widely known: escaping enslavement, leading others to freedom via the Underground Railroad, and tirelessly fighting for change. But a crucial chapter often overlooked is her daring Civil War service as a spy for the US Army, detailed in Dr. Edda L.Fields-Black's groundbreaking book, COMBEE: Harriet Tubman, the Combahee River Raid, and Black Freedom during the Civil War, which won the 2025 Pulitzer Prize in History and the 2025Gilder Lehrman Lincoln Prize. A direct descendant of a soldier who fought in the raid, Fields-Black unveils Tubman's command of spies, scouts, and pilots and intelligence gathering among freedom seekers, which led to a raid that liberated 756 enslaved people from bondage on seven rice plantations. It was the largest slave rebellion in US history. Through unexamined documents, she brings to life the Combahee River Raid and the untold stories of those freed, their resilience, and the lasting impact of Tubman's heroism.

combined_title: This Time *Is* Different: The Challenges—Old and New—of AI in Education: Dr. Kentaro Toyama, U-M School of Information
event_subtitle: Dr. Kentaro Toyama, U-M School of Information
description:
The world's best artificial intelligence systems already exceed us in some ways, and seem poised to surpass us cognitively in every way. Some argue that we are entering a singularity -- a moment when old rules are obsolete; and new ones, impossible to predict. Given that, is there anything at all we can glean about the future of AI and learning? In this talk, I will present a few things we know as a basis for conjecture and make some guesses based on three decades of work in technical AI, societal impacts of digital technology, and faculty governance at a large public university wrestling with this polarizing technology.

Kentaro Toyama is W. K. Kellogg Professor of Community Information at the University of Michigan School of Information, where he researches digital technology's impact on society, especially on its marginalized communities. Previously, Kentaro taught at Ashesi University in Ghana and co-founded Microsoft Research India, where he did research on the applications of digital technology to education and international socio-economic development. He is a fellow of the Dalai Lama Center for Ethics and Transformative Values at MIT; author of Geek Heresy: Rescuing Social Change from the Cult of Technology; and UM Faculty Senate Chair for AY 2026-27.

This event is presented by the GenAI and Human Learning Working Group at the Eileen Lappin Weiser Center for the Learning Sciences.

description:
The Political Ecology Workshop (PEW) is an interdisciplinary space for scholars at all career stages with interests in political ecology and related critical approaches to the study of environment-society interactions. PEW brings together a range of divisions across campus, including Anthropology, History, Environment and Sustainability, Political Science, Sociology, and all Area Studies departments and programs. We have founded a collaborative, multidisciplinary community with a shared investment questioning how environments and societies are co-produced and the ways in which power and inequality impact the dynamics and understandings of this co-production. We have run PEW as an RIW for two years and all the workshops have been possible from our committed participants from diverse fields. This year, we intend to develop our membership further by inviting scholars from broader fields and promoting PEW on listservs across campus.
PEW supports graduate student development, including for earlier-stage students seeking interdisciplinary conversations as they develop environment-society research projects and later-stage students seeking to incorporate political ecology into their work. PEW emphasizes dedicated time for graduate students to receive feedback on their work and facilitates faculty-student mentorship. It allows students to access a range of critical environmental studies perspectives they might not have encountered through coursework or departmental activities, and to grow from the feedback and insight of faculty and peers who share this commitment to interdisciplinary scholarship and professional development.

combined_title: Penny Stamps Speaker Series - Vijay Gupta: Book of Hours
description:
Vijay Gupta is a violinist, curator, and music director who explores the human condition through music. His performing career has taken him from Carnegie Hall — where he debuted at age eight — to county jails, Skid Row shelters, and state psychiatric hospitals, finding in each the same essential questions about what music is for, and who it is for. At eleven, he made his international solo debut with the Israel Philharmonic under Zubin Mehta. At nineteen, he became the youngest violinist ever to join the Los Angeles Philharmonic, where he performed for eleven seasons. The Los Angeles Times has called his playing "brilliant, bold and gripping," and Publishers Weekly praised his memoir Restrung as a "a virtuoso performance” that illustrates how music "reaches the broken places within us and the broken places between us."

A recipient of the MacArthur Fellowship and honoree on the Time 100 Next list, Gupta is the founder and artistic director of Street Symphony, a nonprofit that brings live music into shelters, clinics, county jails, state hospitals, and reentry programs across Los Angeles. Over fifteen years, Street Symphony has delivered more than 3,000 performances and workshops. The New Yorker called it "a formidable new model for how musical institutions should engage with the world around them." 

In addition to his work with Street Symphony, Gupta performs as a soloist and as a founding member of the Darshan Piano Trio. He holds degrees in biology and violin performance and completed graduate study at the Yale School of Music. He has addressed audiences at the Aspen Institute, Mayo Clinic, Harvard Business School, the American Medical Association, and the U.S. Psychiatric Congress, among others. Restrung, his memoir, was published by Grand Central / Da Capo in 2026. 

Joining Gupta for this program is pianist Dominic Cheli, an acclaimed performer whose career has taken him to Carnegie Hall, Walt Disney Concert Hall, and major festivals and orchestras across the United States and abroad. A 2017 first-prize winner of the Concert Artists Guild Competition, Cheli has released acclaimed recordings of works by Clementi, Liszt, Schubert, and Erwin Schulhoff. He is also a member of the Darshan Trio with Gupta and Yoshi Masuda, whose programs bring together chamber music and new music in unexpected and interdisciplinary ways. 

Presented in partnership with the U-M Arts Initiative, the Michigan Arts Festival, and the Ann Arbor Symphony.

Series presenting partners: Detroit PBS, ALL ARTS, and PBS Books. Media partner: Michigan Public.

combined_title: Undergraduate Spiritual Wellness Group
description:
What grounds you? What gives your life meaning? And how do you make space to actually think about those questions in the middle of college life?

Spiritual Wellness Group is an 8-week small-group experience designed to help students slow down, reflect, and develop skills for tending to their inner lives.

Through conversation, reflection, creative activities, and shared practices, participants will strengthen skills in self-awareness, values clarification, deep listening, meaningful conversation, navigating differences, and identifying practices that support their well-being. Together, we’ll explore how our identities, relationships, experiences, beliefs, questions, and values shape the way we understand ourselves and the world around us.

You do not need to identify as religious or spiritual to participate. This is a space for curiosity rather than certainty—where students can ask big questions, learn from one another, and become more intentional about what helps them feel grounded and connected.

By the end of the eight weeks, we hope participants leave with:

A clearer understanding of the values and experiences that shape them
Practical tools for reflection and spiritual well-being
Greater confidence having meaningful conversations across different beliefs and perspectives
Stronger listening and relationship-building skills
New practices for finding grounding, meaning, and connection in everyday life
A community of students willing to engage thoughtfully with some of life's bigger questions

Separate groups are available for undergraduate and graduate students. Light refreshments are provided during sessions, and participants will conclude the eight weeks with a celebration dinner together.

Come as you are. You don't need to have your spirituality figured out—you just need to be willing to explore.

combined_title: Bujinkan Budo Training Session
description:
"Ninpo is the essence of goshinjutsu (self-protection)."
 
During the Fall 2026 semester, Bujinkan Budo Club training will be held on Thursdays from 19:00 - 21:00 (7-9pm) at the Intramural Sports Building (IMSB) in Room MPR B. If you are interested in trying out a class, please send a message through Maize Pages or an email to organizer13@example.edu. Beginners welcome; we train with people across all levels of experience!
 
- Learn self defense and physical coordination through Bujinkan taijiutsu (unarmed combat);
- Training at the Michigan Bujinkan Dojo is supportive and non-competitive, emphasizing relaxed but spirited and disciplined practice;
- Receive mentoring through the senpai/kohai (senior/junior) relationships fostered in the dojo.
 
What to bring: comfortable workout clothes, socks, and a water bottle!
-----
For more information, email us at organizer13@example.edu or checkout our website (www.michiganbujinkan.com), which also includes a training schedule!
